title: Process every file in a folder safely when names contain spaces
summary: Goes through all text files in a folder, including subfolders, and handles each one. File names with spaces, quotes or other odd characters are handled correctly.

warnings: Do not loop with for f in $(find ...) or for f in *.txt when names may contain spaces: the shell splits them into pieces.
find does not sort its output. Pipe the results through sort if you need a fixed order.
Use -print0 together with read -d '' (as in this script) or with xargs -0; the NUL byte cannot appear in a file name.

script.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# process-spaces.sh - process every .txt file in a folder, safely.
# Usage: ./process-spaces.sh DIRECTORY
# Searches the folder recursively. For each .txt file it prints the line
# and word counts. Names with spaces, quotes or even newlines work.

set -euo pipefail

if (( $# != 1 )) || [[ ! -d $1 ]]; then
    echo "usage: $0 DIRECTORY" >&2
    exit 2
fi
DIR=$1

count=0
# find -print0 ends every name with a NUL byte (a byte that never occurs in a
# file name). read -d '' reads up to that NUL, so the name arrives unchanged.
# Never write "for f in $(find ...)": the shell would split names at spaces.
while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
    count=$((count + 1))
    # wc prints the number with padding on some systems; ${x// /} removes spaces.
    lines=$(wc -l < "$file")
    words=$(wc -w < "$file")
    printf '%s: %s lines, %s words\n' "$file" "${lines// /}" "${words// /}"
done < <(find "$DIR" -type f -name '*.txt' -print0)

echo "processed $count file(s)"

prerequisites: A Linux terminal with bash 4 or newer
